title: Henry II's Sons Rise Against Him
text:
Henry II of England ruled an empire stretching from Scotland's border to the Pyrenees, much of it through his wife, Eleanor of Aquitaine. They had four sons who survived to adulthood. Henry gave them titles but kept the power. His eldest, also Henry, was crowned king in 1170 during his father's lifetime, yet had no lands to rule and little money.

In 1173 the Young King fled to the court of his father-in-law, King Louis VII of France. His brothers Richard and Geoffrey joined him, and so did their mother, Eleanor. It was an extraordinary alliance: a queen and three princes in arms against the king, backed by France, Scotland and rebellious barons. Contemporary chroniclers record that Eleanor was captured while trying to reach France, and one says she was dressed in men's clothing.

Henry fought back hard. In July 1174 he did penance at the tomb of Thomas Becket in Canterbury, and that same week the king of Scotland was captured. The rebellion collapsed. Henry forgave his sons, but he kept Eleanor a prisoner for the rest of his reign, about fifteen years.

The family never healed. His sons rebelled again in the following years. In 1189, ill and defeated by Richard and the French king, Henry learned that his favorite son, John, had also gone over to the enemy. He died at Chinon days later.
lesson: Parents who hold back trust and play their children against each other may see them unite against the parents. Real responsibility given early can prevent a revolt later.
people: Henry II, Eleanor of Aquitaine, Henry the Young King, Richard, Geoffrey, John
source: Roger of Howden, Chronica; Ralph of Diceto, Ymagines Historiarum; Gervase of Canterbury, Chronicle; W. L. Warren, Henry II (1973)
